chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn Uthman from Ubaydullah al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"There is no harm in sitting (iq'a) in the prayer between the two prostrations."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This narration is a concession (rukhsah), and the preferable ruling is what we previously mentioned, that one should not sit (iq'a) between the two prostrations. This is confirmed by what was narrated:

key_terms.إِقْعَاء: Sitting on the heels with the buttocks on the ground, a specific posture in prayer
key_terms.الْأَفْضَلُ: The preferable or more virtuous ruling
key_terms.رُخْصَةٌ: A concession or permission in legal rulings, as opposed to the ideal/preferable act

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sit between the two prostrations in Islamic prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the permissibility of sitting (iq'a) between the two prostrations, a practice often associated with the Hanafi school. Shaykh al-Tusi highlights that while valid, this is merely a concession (rukhsa), and the preferred (afdhal) method, as previously detailed in the chapter, is to remain standing or in a different posture, emphasizing the distinction between validity and excellence in Shia jurisprudence.
